episodes.title: The paper your AI never saw
episodes.subtitle: Five real citations. One missing piece of evidence.

scenes.title: Five accurate summaries. What is missing?
narration: Here are five imaginary papers. Every citation is real within our illustration. Every summary is accurate. Would you trust the answer? Now add a sixth paper: the landmark study that the answer never mentioned. Which part of the system failed?
A missing citation alone cannot tell us. Chapter One asks us to follow the evidence before the writing begins.

scenes.title: Follow a documented example
narration: Primo Research Assistant provides a documented example. In the account checked by September twenty twenty-six, a language model converts a question into Boolean variations connected by OR. The query searches the Central Discovery Index and returns up to thirty results.

Embeddings rerank those candidates to identify five sources. Those five become the working set. Only then does GPT four point one Mini write an overview from their abstracts. This is the chapter's dated documentation account, not a fresh test of the service.

scenes.title: Before ranking: can the assistant search it?
narration: Coverage comes first. The chapter's October twenty twenty-six documentation check says the assistant searches CDI metadata and abstracts, subject to exclusions including insufficient metadata or abstracts and some provider collections.

A record in the library's wider discovery system may still fall outside the assistant's searchable scope. A better query or reranker cannot recover a record from a collection the assistant cannot search. These nested sets are schematic, not measured coverage proportions.

scenes.title: Can reordering thirty cards add a thirty-first?
narration: Try the paper-card experiment. Thirty cards enter the candidate set. Reranking can change their order, and selection can keep five. Our gold landmark paper never entered those thirty. Can a better reranker bring it back?

Reordering a fixed set cannot add another member. A new retrieval round could add evidence. Fluent writing cannot establish source-supported coverage of a paper absent from the supplied evidence. Retrieval does not delete the original records from the index.

scenes.title: Locate the loss before naming the failure
narration: Compare three imaginary cases. Paper A is outside the assistant's searchable scope. Paper B reaches the thirty candidates but misses the five-source working set. Paper C reaches the writer but is not cited.

A needs coverage evidence. B needs candidate and selection traces. C needs a comparison between the supplied sources and the answer. If intermediate evidence is hidden, record the uncertainty. Finding a paper in a new direct search does not reconstruct its earlier path.

scenes.title: Six stages, with a controller above them
narration: The chapter maps six possible stages: query transformation; analysis and execution rules; first-stage retrieval; fusion; reranking; and presentation. Fusion combines candidate lists. A controller chooses and sequences the actions. Not every product uses every stage.

No separate fusion stage is documented in the Primo account. Elsevier's twenty twenty-four Scopus AI account describes query variants, vector retrieval and rank fusion. That historical example does not establish the architecture of every later mode.

scenes.title: The writer is a separate machine
narration: Retrieval-augmented generation means retrieval selects evidence and a language model generates an answer conditioned on it. Retrieval limits the supplied evidence. It does not guarantee that every generated statement comes from that evidence.
A model can draw on its parameters, invent a citation or omit a supplied source. Before blaming retrieval or generation for our missing landmark paper, ask what the writer actually received.

episodes.title: A match is not a verdict
episodes.subtitle: The same paper can serve two purposes differently.

scenes.title: Every search condition matches. Enough?
narration: An empirical study passes every condition in a carefully built search. It concerns the right service, the right setting and the right dates. Have we established that it answers the reader's question? Take a moment.
We have established a useful match. Whether it helps depends on what the reader is trying to accomplish. Relevance is a relationship: relevant to someone, for something.

scenes.title: The query represents the information need
narration: The information need is the fuller purpose behind a search. Queries, filters and task briefs can communicate substantial detail about it. A query represents that need; it is not the need itself.

Follow the chain: information need, representation, retrieval signals, retrieved records, human judgement. The system works directly with the middle three. Detailed requests and feedback can help it estimate suitability. The reader still assesses usefulness.

scenes.title: A skilled strategy expresses more
narration: The chapter's hypothetical librarian wants recent empirical studies of generative AI services for research support in academic libraries. The strategy combines alternatives: generative AI or large language models; academic library or university library; research support or research consultation.

Publication dates are limited to twenty twenty-four onwards. These explicit conditions communicate much more than a handful of broad keywords. Now keep the resulting study fixed while we change the purpose.

scenes.title: Same study. Different contribution.
narration: The invented study reports positive participant reactions after a short demonstration of a university library's generative AI research-support service. It matches the search and is topically suitable. For an introductory workshop, it provides a useful example of a service and participants' responses.

For a service-adoption decision, those reactions are insufficient. They do not establish answer accuracy, staff workload or performance in real consultations. The study still contributes evidence about reactions. Its contribution changes with the purpose; its search match has not changed.

scenes.title: Search and judgement improve each other
narration: Targeted follow-up searches can seek accuracy evaluations, workload evidence and real-world use. Then inspect what each study measured, under what conditions, and whether the findings support the decision.

Making every issue a compulsory search condition can also miss useful studies. They may use unexpected terminology or report the issue only in full text. Better searching and relevance judgement work together.

scenes.title: Some criteria belong in screening
narration: Evidence-synthesis searchers call some of these search-resistant concepts. A review criterion may be poorly indexed, inconsistently described or difficult to express as dependable search terms.

A strategy may retrieve a broader set of potentially relevant records and leave some criteria to screening. This is a deliberate division of work between retrieval and assessment. It does not make searching or eligibility criteria unimportant.

scenes.title: Four perspectives, without a fixed ladder
narration: Relevance can concern a system's estimated match, topical suitability, a contribution to the reader's understanding, or usefulness for a task. These are related perspectives, with no single hierarchy among them.

Boolean matching, BM twenty-five, embeddings and neural rerankers help estimate relevance. A high score cannot turn participant reactions into evidence of answer accuracy. Ask what the record contributes to this reader's purpose.

episodes.title: Three clues in a search box
episodes.subtitle: Visible behavior leaves hidden mechanisms open.

scenes.title: Puzzle one: the impossible word
narration: Add an invented nonsense string to a genuine question. If every word is required and the invented string occurs nowhere, what should happen? Under that strict AND assumption, the result set should be empty.

In the chapter's scite screenshot, useful-looking results remain and the interface reports millions. That challenges the strict-AND assumption. It does not prove the system stopped matching words, or identify a semantic retrieval architecture. Our on-screen nonsense token is a teaching illustration.

scenes.title: Puzzle two: millions reported, a thousand viewable
narration: The supplied Google Scholar example reports about nine point four million results for open access. Google's help documentation limits the viewable results for one query to a thousand.

This diagram contains nine thousand four hundred equal marks. Each represents a thousand reported matches. One highlighted mark represents the documented display cap. The reported count does not establish that every matching record was individually scored or ranked. How was the visible fraction chosen?

scenes.title: Puzzle three: the shorter query finds more
narration: In the author's August twenty twenty-six Semantic Scholar observation, the natural-language question returned thirteen results. The shorter, unquoted keyword query returned about thirty-five thousand three hundred. The bars use a labeled logarithmic scale; they are not proportional counts.

The author also judged the question's leading results less relevant, using the known literature and inspected results. That judgement does not follow from the counts alone. The comparison establishes visible behavior. The product's name does not establish its architecture.

scenes.title: What each clue leaves open
narration: The first puzzle leaves an admission rule open. The second leaves ranking and display selection open. The third leaves query interpretation open. Screenshots show outputs; they do not expose a complete pipeline.

The chapter revisits the first two through lexical retrieval in Chapter Four, and the third through mechanisms in Part Two, especially Chapter Seven. Keep the questions open while learning what could explain them. These observations were taken from the chapter, not rerun here.

scenes.title: Two axes—and a third question
narration: The chapter separates output format from retrieval iteration. Across: ranked records or a written answer. Upward: a single or limited pass, or repeated searches. That gives quick search, quick answer, iterative search and deep research.

Neither axis records agency: who chooses the next action? A fixed workflow and an agent can occupy the same box. Repeated retrieval and model-chosen actions are different properties. This diagram maps concepts rather than assigning products to current categories.

scenes.title: Uses an LLM. But where?
narration: A language model can write a query, invent search text such as a pseudo-document, reorder candidates, or control the next retrieval action. Those are uses inside retrieval. It can also write the final answer.
So a vendor saying uses an LLM has located no component. Ask which decision it makes, which evidence it receives and what can be inspected. A polished report alone cannot answer those questions.

scenes.title: Your investigation starts with the working set
narration: Return to the missing landmark paper. Ask whether it was searchable, whether it became a candidate, whether it reached the working set, and whether the writer cited it. Each answer needs different evidence.

Then ask whether the selected papers help with the actual information need. Chapter One has given us the questions. Chapter Two starts with the strictest possible admission rule: words that a record must contain.
